name: Arab nationalism
summary: Arab nationalism holds that the Arabs, defined by a shared language, history and culture rather than by religion or descent, form one nation entitled to one independent state from the Atlantic to the Gulf. It treats the existing borders as the work of imperial partition, Zionism and Israel as an imperial implant on Arab land, and revolution and armed struggle as legitimate means to unity and independence. Its secular mainstream honours Islam as the nation's heritage without making it the basis of the state, and its Ba'th and Nasserist strands tie the national cause to a socialist programme.
scope: The national question as stated by the secular mainstream of the twentieth century: the Ba'th founders (Aflaq and the 1947 constitution, the party's 1970 congress and survey), Nasser's Charter and speeches, al-Husri's language-based definition of the nation as reported by scholarship, and Antonius's history of the movement. Only the doctrine on nation, territory, sovereignty, language, minorities, kin and means is answered; the full economic, welfare and social programmes of the Ba'th and Nasserist regimes are left null unless Aflaq or the Charter state them as part of the national cause. It excludes pan-Islamism, local-state nationalisms and Saddam-era or Assad-era dynastic practice.

notes: Searched all themes in the Ba'th constitution, Aflaq's texts, the Charter (all chapters), two Nasser speeches, the Ba'th survey and 1970 manifesto, and the 1919 Syrian Congress resolutions in Antonius. The Ba'th and Nasserist programmes are answered only where Aflaq or the Charter tie them to the national cause and the Ba'th and Nasser texts share the position (economy, welfare, democracy, religion); positions stated by one strand only (for example the Charter's reparations and foreign aid, or the constitution's anti-tribal and private-school clauses) are null. Strands: the Hashemite revolt and the 1919 Congress wanted a monarchy, the Ba'th and Nasser republics; Aflaq says the army should stay out of government while the Charter has the revolution start in the army; the Ba'th and Nasser differ on a Palestine settlement. Writings of al-Husri himself were not reached and are known through scholarship. Review (2026-10-30): 13 welfare, labour, tax and social answers nulled under the scope rule and 13 single-strand answers (Ba'th-only, or the 1919 Congress only) nulled under the strand rule, for consistency with the pan-arabism re-audit built on the same texts; democracy-best set to +1 low (pass 2 had -1 against the Charter's stated aim) and women-suffrage to +1 medium.
